8fa6376144069885: LONDON: Education Malaysia Global Services (EMGS) has won the Student Support Award at The PIEoneer Awards 2026 for its International Student Arrival Centre (ISAC).
The award gives international recognition to EMGS's efforts to strengthen support for international students.

The recognition comes as EMGS steps up education promotion efforts in the United Kingdom and Ireland amid intensifying competition for international students from established and emerging education destinations.
The award was presented on Sept 4 at London's historic Guildhall during the 10th anniversary of The PIEoneer Awards 2026, known as the "Oscars of international education".
It was received by EMGS chairman Datuk Ahmad Shalimin Ahmad Shaffie and chief executive officer Novie Tajuddin, accompanied by board member Dzariman Ibrahim.

The award recognises ISAC, established in 2018 and described by EMGS as the world's first and only dedicated arrival centre for international students located before immigration clearance at Malaysian international airports.
The shortlist also included established UK organisations UCAS and the UK Council for International Student Affairs (UKCISA).
The recognition comes as Malaysia seeks to diversify its international student population beyond traditional markets.
The country currently has about 167,000 international students, mainly from China, Indonesia, Bangladesh, India and Pakistan, with EMGS setting an ambition of reaching 500,000 by 2035.
Shalimin said EMGS's integrated role in promoting higher education, processing student visas and monitoring international students gave Malaysia an advantage in managing the student journey.

"The United Kingdom was previously among the four biggest countries in the world in higher education. And now Malaysia is one of the new 14 big players in higher education, and we have demonstrated our commitment.

"We are the only country with an implementing agency that serves as a one-stop centre. EMGS is the sole implementing agency that not only promotes higher education, but also processes student visas and takes care of and monitors international students in Malaysia."
The UK and Ireland are among the markets Malaysia is targeting as it seeks to diversify its international student base beyond traditional recruitment markets.
EMGS is using a combination of education fairs, community engagement and targeted outreach to introduce Malaysia's higher education opportunities to prospective students and their families.

As part of the campaign, EMGS held an engagement session at London Central Mosque on Friday, where participants discussed higher education opportunities in Malaysia, affordability, student support, visa guidance and facilities catering to diverse cultural and religious needs.

Novie said feedback from the session indicated that the cost of higher education in the UK was a growing concern among some families, creating an opportunity for Malaysia to position itself as an alternative.
"We found a niche market in the Muslim community. Many of them said studying in the UK at school level is still affordable, but when they move on to higher education, they find it expensive.
"So we are stepping in because we believe studying in Malaysia is a solution for UK and Ireland passport holders," he said.
Students who attended the session said studying in Malaysia would offer both an overseas educational and cultural experience.
One student, Yasser Banga, said: "It seems really interesting because you get to study abroad and it's good for culture and also for experience. So I would really like to be part of this experience."
Another student, Darry Collard, said: "I think it's a very unique experience. It's like a once-in-a-lifetime thing, so I think it's pretty much worth it for foreign students to study in Malaysia."
EMGS also took part in the Malaysia Carnival at Brickendonbury as part of its wider UK outreach, with its booth drawing members of the community seeking information about studying in Malaysia.

Organised by the High Commission of Malaysia in London, the annual carnival attracted more than 3,000 visitors and showcased Malaysian culture, food, performances and tourism alongside education opportunities.
Malaysian High Commissioner to the UK Datuk Indera Dr Azfar Mohamad Mustafar said Malaysian students already studying in the UK could also help raise awareness of Malaysia among local communities.
"In the context of education, Malaysian students studying in the UK can become 'duta kecil', introducing our culture to communities in the UK.
"Through this approach, I believe we can link it to our efforts to promote Malaysia as an education hub in the Southeast Asian region," he said.

The campaign is part of Malaysia's longer-term effort to diversify its international student population and strengthen engagement with prospective students, parents, universities and communities in new markets.
Novie said the PIEoneer recognition for ISAC underscored the importance of placing student welfare at the centre of Malaysia's international education strategy.
"This achievement shows the world what Malaysia is capable of delivering when innovation and student care move together.
"We believe ISAC has set a strong global benchmark and can serve as an example to other countries of what is possible when the international student experience is made a priority.
"Ultimately, everything we do must deliver meaningful benefits to international students," he said.

2529163428335315: GEORGE TOWN: The United States government should take legal action against Pas president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang if his claims of US political interference in Malaysia are false, said DAP lawmaker RSN Rayer.
The Jelutong member of parliament said Hadi had made a serious allegation that US representatives had approached Pas leaders and offered assistance to topple the Malaysian government.
Rayer said Hadi had also claimed that the matter involved senior Pas leaders and that he later met the US ambassador.
He said the claims concerned national security and alleged interference by a foreign power in Malaysia's constitutional and democratic affairs.
Rayer said the US Embassy had rejected the allegation, saying the US had never sought to determine Malaysia's political leadership and that reports suggesting otherwise were false.
He said there were 2 possibilities: either Hadi was telling the truth, or he was not.
"If Hadi is telling the truth, then the United States has some very serious questions to answer.
"However, if Washington's denial is accurate, the US should consider legal action rather than simply issuing a diplomatic denial.
"This is a very serious matter. A mere lip service diplomatic denial by the US is not enough," he said today.
Rayer said legal action against Hadi, if his claims were untrue, would allow Malaysians to determine who was telling the truth.
The US Embassy in Kuala Lumpur today denied ever seeking to determine Malaysia's political leadership, calling any suggestion otherwise false.
The statement followed a claim by Hadi that a US Embassy representative had once asked him who the party proposed as prime minister.
Hadi said the meeting took place when Pas was still part of the Pakatan Rakyat coalition, around the time of then US president Barack Obama's visit to Malaysia.
He made the claim during his winding-up speech at the party's 72nd Pas Annual Muktamar in Kota Baru yesterday.

1d067bcb81ece1e4: OSLO: German startup Isar Aerospace on Sunday said it would rapidly expand satellite deployments after the first orbital launch of its Spectrum rocket from Arctic Norway, a milestone for Europe's efforts to secure independent access to space.

The uncrewed Spectrum became the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe, marking a breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches.
"Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry," Isar co-founder and CEO Daniel Metzler told reporters.
He said privately owned Isar remains well-funded and that an initial public offering "is not on the table".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hailed Saturday's launch in a statement, calling it "the beginning of a new era".
Merz visited Isar's launch site in March, underscoring Europe's efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under US president Donald Trump.
Blasting off from Norway's Arctic Andoya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment, according to Isar.
The rocket is designed to serve the growing market for small and medium-sized payloads.
"Europe's independent access to space just got a major boost," EU defence and space commissioner Andrius Kubilius wrote on social media platform X.
It was Isar's second launch, coming 18 months after the company's first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site. No one was injured.
Isar said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting around 40 launches a year.
The German company is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada, and said on Sunday this could be ready for lift-offs in 2028.
Saturday's launch was intended as "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload," the Bavarian company said.

"The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoya strengthens Norwegian and European security in the turbulent times we live in," said Norway's minister of industry and commerce, Cecilie Myrseth.

Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk's SpaceX, which launches from the US, and French ArianeGroup, a joint venture between Airbus and Safran that uses a spaceport in South America's French Guiana.
SpaceX, a company spanning rockets, satellites and AI, in June listed on the Nasdaq exchange in a record initial public offering.

Sweden, with its Esrange launch site, and Britain with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, are the nearest rivals to the Norwegian site, all of which aim to give Europe greater autonomy in space flights.
Isar last week said it had secured about €200 million (US$232 million) from the European Space Agency to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure.
6ab44d78dbe0113e: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysians stranded in Indonesia following flight cancellations caused by the eruption of Anak Krakatau have been forced to incur additional expenses, with return airfares reportedly rising by as much as threefold.

Dhia Adawiah, 26, from Kuala Lumpur, was scheduled to return to Malaysia at 5am today on a Batik Air flight after travelling alone to Jakarta on Sept 4 to attend a concert by Indonesian music group Kahitna.
She said a one-way flight to Malaysia for tomorrow cost at least RM1,071, in addition to RM150 for another night's accommodation.
"All the flight ticket prices have increased threefold. When I checked, the cheapest flight available for tomorrow was RM1,071, on top of an additional RM150 for one night at a hotel.
"For now, I have to wait and see how the situation develops. If flights are able to operate tomorrow, I will book one immediately," she said when contacted.
The marketing executive said the disruption had also affected her work, as she had several matters that needed to be settled upon her return to Malaysia.
"It is difficult because I have a lot of work that needs to be completed. This is the first time in my life that I have experienced a situation like this," she said.
She said the airline had yet to respond, forcing her to apply for a refund. She plans to purchase another flight ticket once conditions permit.

Another Malaysian, Fatin Nur Athirah Mohd Rodzi, from Shah Alam, said she was scheduled to return on a KLM Royal Dutch Airlines flight at 7.30pm today. However, she received a notification at 8am that the flight had been cancelled.
She said she had travelled to Jakarta with five other family members last Thursday for work-related purposes.
"I am worried because my children are supposed to return to school tomorrow and I also need to get back to work.
"It is stressful because this is the first time I have ever been stranded in another country," she said.
She said her family was stranded at Terminal 3 of Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and had sought clarification, but the counters for the airline concerned and AirAsia had yet to open.
"The airport is crowded, with many Malaysians stranded here. I also noticed a lot of ash covering vehicles.
"I hope the situation stabilises soon, flight operations return to normal and alternative flights can be arranged so that we can return home as soon as possible," she said.
The eruption of Anak Krakatau has continued since Friday, causing volcanic ash to spread and prompting six airports to suspend flight operations.
The disruption has also affected domestic and international flights, including routes connecting Jakarta with Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, Hong Kong, Sydney, Seoul/Incheon, Doha and Amsterdam.
3c893b599ace2cd3: LUMUT: Perbezaan pandangan berhubung peruntukan Kementerian Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah (KKDW) yang diselia Kementerian Kewangan (MoF) tidak menjejaskan keutuhan kerjasama politik antara Pakatan Harapan (PH) dan Barisan Nasional (BN), kata Ketua Pemuda PKR Kamil Munim.

Kamil yang juga setiausaha politik kepada menteri kewangan berkata perbincangan di peringkat MoF akan memberi tumpuan kepada penelitian semula keperluan peruntukan serta memastikan keutamaan diberikan kepada projek pembangunan masyarakat desa yang berimpak tinggi.

Isu berkenaan menarik perhatian susulan kenyataan berbeza antara pemimpin kedua-dua gabungan berhubung peruntukan projek pembangunan luar bandar, yang mencetuskan spekulasi mengenai keharmonian hubungan politik PH-BN menjelang PRN Melaka.

Zahid berkata masalah yang berlaku itu memberi kesan kepada kontraktor yang melaksanakan projek kerajaan, selain menegaskan keperluan menyelesaikan isu berkenaan supaya masalah bayaran tidak berlarutan.

Ketua Setiausaha Perbendaharaan Johan Mahmood Merican pada 2 Sept memaklumkan tidak ada sebarang sekatan terhadap peruntukan KKDW bagi projek jalan luar bandar dan keseluruhan peruntukan bagi projek berkenaan telah disalurkan.
Beliau berkata kekangan dalam proses pembayaran kepada kontraktor berpunca daripada peruntukan tahun semasa yang hampir keseluruhannya telah dibelanjakan.

Dalam perkembangan lain, Kamil menyifatkan cadangan Ahli Parlimen Kepong Lim Lip Eng supaya kerajaan mempertimbangkan pengembalian Cukai Barang dan Perkhidmatan (GST) sebagai pandangan peribadi yang dikemukakan berteraskan hujah serta analisis sendiri.

Beliau berkata pendirian kerajaan ketika ini kekal untuk meneruskan pelaksanaan Cukai Jualan dan Perkhidmatan (SST), dengan sebarang perubahan dasar perlu mengambil kira keadaan serta keperluan semasa.

"Jadi dalam keadaan ini, dasar itu boleh berubah mengikut keadaan dan juga waktu tetapi buat masa hari ini, setakat ini, pendekatan dan juga keputusan kerajaan ialah untuk terus dengan dasar yang sedia ada," katanya.
Semalam, Lim menyarankan kerajaan mengembalikan GST dan melaksanakan sistem percukaian itu dengan sewajarnya, jika ia lebih berkesan berbanding SST.
91f402d61563eb6a: KUALA LUMPUR: A search and rescue (SAR) operation to locate six people, including four family members and two mountain guides feared lost in the Gua Musang jungle, will begin tomorrow with helicopter assistance.

Fire and Rescue Department director-general Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohammad said a helicopter will be deployed from Sungai Siput, Perak, in the morning to conduct aerial reconnaissance over suspected locations and track the group's intended route.
"We have formed a SAR team, and operations will commence tomorrow," he said when contacted today.
He said firefighters have assembled in Gerik, Perak, believed to be the exit point for the group, to plan search sectors and coordinate ground logistics tonight.
The search efforts will be supported by a team of mountain guides already on-site to help identify and mark potential trails used by the victims.
The group of six reportedly entered the forest via Pos Dakoh, Lojing, Gua Musang, on Aug 29.
Gua Musang district police chief Superintendent Sik Choon Foo said family members lodged a missing person report in Selangor after the group failed to emerge as scheduled on Sept 3.
A cross-check with the Forestry Department indicated that last contact with the group placed them in the Perak forest reserve before communication was lost.
The group possesses valid permits to enter the forest reserve and was scheduled to exit at Pos Kemar, Perak.
Gua Musang police remain on standby should confirmation arise that the hikers are within Kelantan borders.

72002d180906febb: KANAZAWA, Sept 6 — In the historic Japanese city of Kanazawa, craftsmen painstakingly shape and slice blocks of ice destined to chill negronis in some of the world’s trendiest bars.
The men work for Kuramoto Ice, a century-old company in Ishikawa on the Sea of Japan coast and one of dozens of Japanese firms producing ultra-clear, premium ice.
This luxury product, believed by those in the industry to melt more slowly than regular blocks, is a staple of Japan’s cocktail culture.
But its popularity is also spilling over to bars abroad, from the United States to Australia, who pay as much as 200 yen (US$1.25) per cube.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Ice spheres sit in a basket after being cut at the Kuramoto Ice factory. — AFP pic
Kuramoto Ice is of the country’s few international exporters, and has seen total sales more than double since exports began in 2019.
“We take our time and freeze water slowly, keeping it in motion... That’s how we end up with good ice,” Kazuhiko Kuramoto, the firm’s fifth-generation head, told AFP at their Kanazawa factory.
“My heart leaps with joy when I see ice that looks like a jewel,” said the 41-year-old, as he poured cold hojicha tea into a glass filled with a large, clear sphere.

Using a technique that originally came from the United States, specialist Japanese ice makers freeze water over a period of 48 to 72 hours, far longer than the few hours typically required for homemade ice or the 30 minutes it takes industrial ice machines.

As freezing begins and the ice forms from outside in, various impurities in the water get pushed towards the centre. But the Japanese method involves removing that tainted water and replacing it with a fresh batch. Constant stirring helps remove air bubbles, resulting in completely transparent ice, known as “junpyo” in Japanese.
Although there is little scientific evidence, it’s said the technique also results in a colder, denser product that will cool rather than dilute a cocktail.
Native — a trendy bar in Singapore that made this year’s Asia’s 50 Best Bars list — imports around 900 kilograms of ice from Kuramoto each year.
“Local ice is more economical, but Kuramoto Ice is clearer, denser and melts more slowly,” co-owner Yong Wei told AFP.
‘Lingering aftertaste’

In Kanazawa, workers dressed in full-body overalls haul large blocks of ice across the factory floor, before starting on the delicate work of carving perfect spheres, cubes and rectangular blocks with cut corners.
Once packaged, the finished products — which can be made to precisely fit any glass — are stored in a room at minus 10 degrees before shipment.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This picture taken on June 15, 2026 shows the Kuramoto Ice factory in Kanazawa. — AFP pic

Boss Kuramoto is not blind to the environmental cost of transporting cubes of ice thousands of kilometres across the world, but insisted that small goods like his have a relatively low environmental impact.

He said he had dreamed of reaching American bars since visiting Las Vegas more than a decade ago and realising low-quality ice that melts easily and waters down the flavour was being used in expensive cocktails.
The time-consuming ice-making technique often used in Japan, which tends to produce a higher quality product, had largely been phased out in the US.
At a Hilton Hotel bar near Tokyo, bartender Shingo Miyachi prepares a negroni with one of Kuramoto Ice’s big, clear cubes.
The ice fits perfectly in the glass, and its clarity makes it almost invisible.
“Ice really has a huge impact on the taste of a cocktail,” Miyachi told AFP.
If it melts, “it especially affects the lingering aftertaste once you’ve taken a sip.”
Ice handling is considered an essential skill for Japanese bartenders, who often begin their training by learning to break it with precision.

“When you look at the ice and see the level of attention to detail, you can pretty much tell how seriously the bartender takes the flavour of the cocktail and how much care they’ve put into it,” he explained.
“A cocktail only really comes into being when the glass, the ice, and the liquid become one as a single unified whole.” — AFP
b9570a1508638677: PERPIGNAN (France), Sept 6 — Agence France-Presse photographer Luis Tato on Saturday won the top prize at the prestigious Visa Pour l’Image photojournalism festival in Perpignan, France.
Spaniard Tato won the Visa d’Or prize for news photography for his coverage of Generation Z protests in Madagascar.
His work on the story had already been recognised at the World Press Photo Awards in April.
Accepting the award, 37-year-old Tato paid tribute to festival founder Jean-Francois Leroy, who died on Monday.
Leroy, he said, had given him an early break in 2018 when he showed his work for the first time.
Tato also acknowledged the young people of Madagascar, who “knew how important it was that their story be told”.
Agence France-Presse photographer Luis Tato on Saturday won the top prize at the prestigious Visa Pour l’Image photojournalism festival in Perpignan, France. — AFP pic

In September 2025, student-led protests erupted across Madagascar over failing public services, corruption, and economic hardship. When President Andry Rajoelina dissolved his government but refused to resign, demonstrations intensified.

“I think this global movement of young people who are trying to redefine democracy and transform their societies is a very interesting dynamic, which fascinates me both as a photographer and as someone who seeks to understand the world we live in,” said Tato.
Based in Kenya, Tato covers east Africa and the Indian Ocean region for AFP.

His work has already been recognised in several photography competitions, including three times at the World Press Photo awards; at the Pictures of the Year International, Sony World Photography Awards and NPPA Best of Photojournalism.
The exhibitions featured at the Visa pour L’Image event are on display in venues around Perpignan until September 13. — AFP

2e8a8ddb954ff46a: KUALA LUMPUR: A 62-year-old man set fire to a car in Cheras after hallucinating that a foreign man and a woman were having sex inside the vehicle.
The incident occurred at Jalan Midah 1, Cheras, on Monday.
The man allegedly saw the pair entering the car and knocked on its door, believing someone was inside, before throwing a flammable substance under the vehicle, causing it to catch fire.
Cheras district police chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Rosdi Daud said police arrested the man, a plumber, in Desa Tun Razak less than 24 hours after the incident.
"Police found a bottle containing a liquid believed to be thinner in the suspect's vehicle, which is believed to have been used as an accelerant.
"The suspect was also believed to be under the influence of drugs at the time," he said in a statement today.
Rosdi said the suspect had no previous criminal record, but an initial urine screening tested positive for methamphetamine and amphetamine.

He said the suspect was remanded for three days from Wednesday to Friday to assist investigations under Section 435 of the Penal Code, which carries a maximum 14-year jail term and a fine upon conviction.
The investigation paper was referred to the deputy public prosecutor's office, which instructed police to charge the suspect under the same section.
The man was subsequently charged at the Jalan Duta magistrate's court in Kuala Lumpur on Friday. He pleaded not guilty.
The court ordered him to be remanded at Sungai Buloh Prison pending mention of the case on Oct 26.

At the climax of the finals, Joheirry Mola Dominguez of the Dominican Republic was crowned Miss World 2026, while Elisabeth Reynes Alabern of Spain secured second place.
Taanusiya qualified for the top six after winning the Beauty With A Purpose (BWAP) segment, edging out Zimbabwe's candidate Brunette Makanyiso.

The core charity-based segment focuses on contestants championing humanitarian, educational, and healthcare projects. Following her win, Taanusiya will join Dominguez on a global tour to carry out humanitarian duties.
Dressed in a pink gown by Vietnamese designer Minh Tuan Couture, Taanusiya impressed the judges during the question-and-answer round with her response on environmental protection.

Drawing on her experience as a teacher, she highlighted the importance of cultivating environmental awareness from an early age through tree planting, teaching children growth, patience, and responsibility.

"I want to be the sort of teacher who offers students, no matter their background, the seeds to plant that take time to grow. When you do that, you will influence many others around the world," she said.
Her performance drew widespread praise from beauty pageant fans locally and abroad. Her third-place finish matched Malaysia's best achievement set by Lina Teoh in 1998.

Taanusiya previously gained attention by speaking fluently in Malay, English, Mandarin, and Tamil during the Head-to-Head Challenge for Asia and Oceania on Aug 23. She also actively promotes community initiatives through Be The Change Malaysia.
9576ffcad4fdc14e: KUALA LUMPUR: Rohingya refugees holding cards issued by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are not classified as undocumented migrants and do not fall under the jurisdiction of the Immigration Department.
Its director-general Datuk Zakaria Shaaban said UNHCR cardholders are afforded immunity from enforcement action over offences involving travel documents or invalid passes.
"Rohingya are not the same as undocumented migrants. Those holding UNHCR cards cannot be prosecuted for immigration offences such as overstaying or not having valid travel documents and passes.
"However, they remain subject to other laws enforced by other enforcement agencies," he said when contacted for comment on the status of Rohingya refugees.

On enforcement against undocumented migrants in general, Zakaria welcomed information and complaints from the public to enable the Immigration Department to investigate and conduct operations in areas suspected of having undocumented migrants.
"Immigration enforcement is based on complaints, intelligence and information from the public.
"All information and complaints received will be investigated.
"However, members of the public are advised not to take matters into their own hands, but to hand over any information to the authorities," he said.
faad480ba86e4168: JAKARTA: Two more airports in Indonesia have been closed, bringing the total to eight, as volcanic ash from Anak Krakatau disrupted air travel, affecting about 150,000 passengers and 467 flights.

The latest closures were of Taufik Kiemas airport and Atung Bungsu airport, both in South Sumatra. Others closed earlier were in Java: Soekarno-Hatta International and Halim Perdanakusuma in Jakarta, Radin Inten II in Lampung, Husein Sastranegara in West Java, Budiarto and Pondok Cabe in Banten.

Indonesia's transport minister said volcanic ash had been detected moving east at 5 knots at 15,000 feet, after winds had earlier carried it west towards the Indian Ocean. Tests were being conducted every 30 minutes at airports further east across Java to monitor whether the ash was spreading or receding.
Alternative airports have been opened at Kertajati, Semarang, Juanda, Yogyakarta and Solo for 24-hour operations.
The closures affected 409 domestic services and 58 international flights.
17465fe97bdd254f: TEHERAN: Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf threatened on Sunday to launch swifter and more forceful responses to US attacks, after an exchange of fire in which Teheran targeted American warships and the US attacked Iranian tankers.

"The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end," said Ghalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that "any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response."

Saturday's attacks included the Revolutionary Guards saying they targeted a US naval drone, three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and US vessels elsewhere, as well as a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) had said its forces "disabled" two Iranian oil tankers off Iran's Kharg island and "completely destroyed" an unladen Iranian crude oil tanker in the Sea of Oman.
In its statement, CENTCOM said American warships had "successfully evaded" Iran's attacks.
Iran has largely blocked passage through the Strait of Homruz since the outbreak of war on Feb 28.
Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and last month announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign on Iran aimed at strangling its already battered economy.
In his speech, Ghalibaf called on authorities to better manage Iranian imports to confront what he called the US campaign "seeking to paralyse the supply cycle and energy management."
On Sunday, Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said Teheran through this war was seeking to inflict economic damage on the US.
"If America wants to inflict one dollar of economic damage on Iran, it inflicts tens of dollars of damage on itself," he added.
f03973cf6bcb6cd5: SEPANG, Sept 6 — Passengers stranded for over 12 hours at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 1 following flight cancellations to Jakarta hope the situation will resolve quickly so they can resume their journeys.
Redy Dwi Lingga, 21, said he and his friend arrived as early as 6 am for an 8 am flight to Jakarta, only to end up waiting for hours after being informed that their flight was cancelled.
“I didn’t expect this to happen. I came early in the morning for an 8 am flight, but ended up waiting for hours at the airport.
“I hope everything goes smoothly and the weather clears up so that flights can resume quickly,” he told Bernama.
He also urged the authorities to provide updates on flight schedules as soon as possible for the welfare of passengers.
According to MAHB, the cancellations reported by airlines as at noon today involved flights scheduled between 6.45am and 11.55pm. — Bernama pic
Meanwhile, Octavia Suci Siregar, 18, said her flight scheduled to depart at 9.55 pm today was also cancelled, leaving her waiting at a designated area in KLIA Terminal 1.
“I hope everything gets resolved quickly so we can continue our journey to Jakarta. Right now, we are just waiting for further information from the airline,” she said.
Octavia also urged airlines to promptly provide flight schedule updates to allow passengers to plan their journeys accordingly.

“I am travelling alone, so I will remain at KLIA Terminal 1 until the airline provides a new flight date. I hope flights resume soon as I really want to return to Jakarta,” said Octavia, who arrived in Malaysia last week.

Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) said 31 flights to Jakarta across all airports nationwide were cancelled today following the temporary closure of Soekarno-Hatta International Airport due to volcanic ash from the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau.
According to MAHB, the cancellations reported by airlines as at noon today involved flights scheduled between 6.45am and 11.55pm.
The airport operator explained that Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) recorded the highest number of cancellations with 21 flights, comprising 15 at Terminal 1 and six at Terminal 2.

Mount Anak Krakatau, located in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra, continued erupting through Saturday, with authorities reporting lava fountains and loud booming and rumbling sounds audible from an observation post.
The eruption began at 11.07 pm local time on Friday and persisted throughout observations from midnight to 6 am yesterday.

Indonesia’s Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation reported volcanic ash reaching heights of 6,000 metres on the Java side of the volcano, while ash plumes extended up to 15,000 metres over parts of Sumatra and Banten province in Java.
Flight operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport were suspended until 1.30 pm local time today (2.30 pm Malaysian time). — Bernama
ee7f8319c7245e4d: KUALA LUMPUR: Qualifier Shahadzryl Suhaime hopes to get called up to the national setup after claiming two under-13 titles at the Lee Chong Wei Cup today.
Shahadzryl, who is from Pahang, claimed the boys' singles title after coming from behind to beat Penang's Jorus Lee 12-15, 15-12, 15-12 in the final at the Stadium Juara.
He then teammed up with Gan Giap Han to beat Sarawak's Ahmad Aniq Rafiq Mohd Zariffi-Lucas Ho 15-12, 15-12 in the boys' doubles final.
The diminutive Shahadzryl, who has been paired with the much-taller Giap Han since they were 11, said they knew they had to be aggressive in the final.

"My goal from the very start of the week was to win both titles though I knew there would be tough opposition along the way," said Shahadzryl, 13, who had to go through the qualifiers in both the singles and doubles events.
"For the doubles final, the goal was to avoid lifting too many shots and just attack as much as possible.
"Of course I am very happy to end the tournament as the champion in both events."
Giap Han and Shahadzryl, who are both Bukit Jalil Sports School students, hope to join the national team in the future.
"I would be really happy if they (BAM) offer me a trial," said Shahadzryl.
"All of the players who are in the BAM setup are performing at a high level and I would love to try and get in."
"It is also my dream to join the national setup. I want to represent Malaysia one day," added Giap Han.
The Lee Chong Wei Cup, which is in its inaugural edition this year, has been billed as Malaysia's premier youth badminton tournament, offering a RM104,000 prize pool across 13 categories this season.

19d615b256b1edfa: PETALING JAYA: Empat ahli keluarga, dua malim gunung antara enam individu dikhuatiri hilang selepas memasuki kawasan hutan melalui Pos Dakoh, Lojing, Gua Musang, 29 Ogos lalu.

Ketua Polis Gua Musang, Sik Choon Foo, berkata pihaknya menerima laporan berkaitan kehilangan itu daripada ahli keluarga kumpulan berkenaan di Selangor hari ini, selepas mereka gagal keluar dari hutan mengikut tarikh dijadualkan pada 3 Sept.
Katanya, hasil semakan dengan Jabatan Perhutanan mendapati hubungan terakhir dengan kumpulan itu menunjukkan mereka berada di kawasan hutan Perak, sebelum terputus hubungan.

“Pada masa ini kita sedang berurusan dengan pihak Perak untuk mendapatkan pengesahan kerana berdasarkan hubungan terakhir, mereka sudah berada di kawasan hutan Perak dan bukan lagi di kawasan Kelantan,” katanya kepada Bernama.
Sik berkata, kumpulan itu mempunyai permit memasuki kawasan hutan dan menggunakan khidmat dua malim gunung.
Beliau berkata, kumpulan itu memasuki hutan melalui Pos Dakoh dan dijadualkan keluar di Pos Kemar, Perak.

“Buat masa ini kita belum menjalankan operasi di sebelah Kelantan kerana semakan menunjukkan mereka telah melepasi sempadan negeri. Kita hanya bersiap sedia sekiranya terdapat perkembangan atau pengesahan bahawa mereka berada di kawasan Kelantan,” katanya.
Sik berkata, polis turut menyemak maklumat berkaitan kenderaan yang digunakan kumpulan itu, termasuk kemungkinan mereka menggunakan kenderaan sewa atau pengangkutan disediakan malim gunung.
8e332d3791bb2ebc: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 6 — The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) has arrested two individuals, including a former director-general of a statutory body with the title ‘Datuk’, over alleged misappropriation, abuse of power, and corruption.
The suspects, aged in their 50s and 60s, were detained around 4 pm today after arriving to provide their statements at the MACC headquarters in Putrajaya.
A source said the suspects are believed to have abused their power in appointing a company for a project and in the sale of land owned by the statutory body.

“Both individuals are suspected of involvement in the sale of land owned by the statutory body to a company linked to the developer without the knowledge of the Board of Directors and its subsidiary,” the source said.
Both suspects will be taken to the Putrajaya Magistrate’s Court tomorrow for a remand application.
MACC Chief Commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman, when contacted, confirmed the arrests and said the case is being investigated under Section 16 of the MACC Act 2009. — Bernama
fe226105f28d01cf: RIYADH, Sept 6 — Eight Islamic and Arab countries on Sunday condemned plans voiced by Israeli government ministers for the removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, saying the designs jeopardise a US-backed peace in the territory.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday Israel had plans to remove Palestinians from Gaza but was waiting for US approval on where to displace the territory’s population.

A day later, Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of the roughly two million residents over the following six years.

The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia and Turkey said they condemned in “the strongest terms” the “plans and mechanisms they proposed aimed at forcibly expelling Palestinians from their land”.
The ministers warned of “grave consequences of transforming calls for forced displacement into declared policy or practical measures”.

“Such measures directly challenge international efforts to achieve peace, particularly President Donald Trump’s comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza, which includes a firm rejection of forced displacement,” they added referring to a US-backed, October 2025 peace plan for Gaza.

On Saturday the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, denied there was an Israeli plan to force Palestinians out of Gaza. — AFP
1f9b7b0b54d06648: GEORGE TOWN, Sept 6 — Six flights from Penang International Airport to Jakarta, Indonesia were cancelled today following the temporary closure of Soekarno-Hatta International Airport due to volcanic dust from the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau.
Penang Tourism and Creative Economy Committee chairman Wong Hon Wai said the cancellations involved AirAsia, TransNusa and Batik Air flights and affected about 1,000 passengers.

“Flights will depend on the situation at the airport in Jakarta and we advise passengers to follow the latest announcements from their airlines,” he said when contacted by Bernama today, adding that the state authorities will monitor developments about flight disruptions.
Checks by Bernama at the Penang International Airport found that passenger movement was normal at the arrival and departure halls.
Mount Anak Krakatau, located in the Sunda Straits between Jawa and Sumatera began erupting at 11.07 pm local time on Friday and has continued to do so from midnight till 6 am yesterday.
Flight operations at the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport have been suspended till 1.30 pm local time today (2.30 pm, Malaysia time). — Bernama
def1d5bf5014afcf: KUALA LUMPUR: Schoolboy shuttler Shahadzryl Suhaime was the standout performer at the inaugural Lee Chong Wei Cup tournament, becoming the sole player to capture two titles at the tournament today.
The 13-year-old from Bukit Jalil Sports School showed remarkable physical resilience throughout the tournament, having fought all the way from the qualifying rounds, which began on Aug 29.
Shahadzryl kicked off his final-day triumph in the under-13 boys' singles, showing composure to bounce back from a game down to defeat Penang's Jorus Lee 12-15, 15-12, 15-12.
He maintained his momentum in the under-13 boys' doubles, pairing up with Gan Giap Han, to see off Sarawak's Ahmad Aniq Rafiq Mohd Zariffi-Lucas Ho 15-12, 15-12.
Despite the tight schedule throughout the nine-day event and coming from qualifiers, Shahadzryl said that winning both events was always his primary objective.
"From the start of the tournament, I already aimed for two championships," he told reporters.

Shahadzryl, from Kuantan, said he started playing badminton at the age of five and idolises national badminton legend Lee Chong Wei. He has set his sights firmly on his ultimate goal of earning a place in the Badminton Association of Malaysia national setup.
His doubles partner Gan, 13, said their winning mindset was established well before stepping onto the court; he hoped to join the BAM setup, too, in the future.
Shahadzryl won RM2,000 as boys’ singles under-13 champion, and RM3,000 with Gan in the under-13 doubles.
59a749bbd151775f: KYIV: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Kyiv Sunday for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after holding talks with Russia's Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on ending more than four years of war between the neighbours.
US president Donald Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner had visited Moscow several times but had not held talks in Kyiv - hit by deadly Russian strikes since 2022.
They are due to meet with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky. An AFP reporter in Kyiv saw the American envoys arrive by train.
They are hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe's worst conflict since WWII, after a summer of escalation.
Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin on Saturday to "advance president Trump's agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War," a White House official said in a statement to AFP.
"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," it said.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks "extremely frank", saying the Americans "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement", but did not elaborate.
"The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was "confident" it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine," Ushakov added.
Both Russia and Ukraine have vowed not to strike each other's capitals for three days to allow for the negotiations to take place.
It was Kushner and Witkoff's eighth visit to Moscow during the war - but it is their first in the Ukrainian capital, hit by deadly Russian strikes throughout the war.
Russia's TASS news agency reported early Sunday that Witkoff and Kushner had arrived in Rzeszow in Poland on their way to Kyiv.
Zelensky on Sunday said Ukraine was "ready for the conversation."
"Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," the wartime leader said on social media ahead of their visit.
The country's airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war in February 2022 and visiting leaders have been arriving by train.
For many Ukrainians, hopes of a breakthrough remain slim.
"At this point it doesn't give me any hope. There have already been too many negotiations," Yaroslav, a 29-year-old Kyiv resident, told AFP.
Putin thanks Trump
In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv - a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war.
"We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves," Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being "not simple".
Of the envoys' trip to Kyiv, he said: "No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial".
Trump said on Friday his envoys were bringing a "proposal" to end fighting.
"We have an idea for peace," he said, without elaborating.
US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war, and peace efforts have stalled in part because of Washington's war with Iran.
Russia occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Limited truce
Both Moscow and Kyiv committed to suspending strikes as the negotiations took place.
"The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Zelensky said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow," Zelensky said.
However, fighting continued elsewhere. Ukraine's air force said Russia attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it had shot down 258 drones.
On Saturday, Putin said he had "noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced" its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
However, Kyiv said that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country Saturday - including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv.

7f5a4b9f58dd0734: KOTA KINABALU, Sept 6 — Students who face bullying are urged to come forward immediately and report the incidents to their teachers, parents and authorities.

State Education Department deputy director (student development sector) Muddin Beting stressed that victims of abuse must stand firm on the truth and justice to prevent their peers from suffering the same fate in the future.
“Get help urgently so that justice can be done.

“And do not, at any time, bully, abuse or demean your schoolmates,” he said in officiating at the ‘Kesedaran Aerobeat Bully 2026’ programme carried out by the National Consumer Action Council (MTPN) Sabah here on Sunday.

According to Muddin, schools are supposed to be where human capital is developed and thus, students should not attend school with feelings of worry for their safety due to the risk of abuse and bullying.
Adding on, he said the Education Department commended MTPN Sabah for organising the anti-bullying programme, which he hoped would bring positive results throughout the state.
In this respect, he gave assurance that the department would continue supporting the council in running similar programmes in the future.
Meanwhile, MTPN Sabah Youth chairman Calvin Choo stressed that all students have the right to feel safe at all times.
“We want to share the message that the threat of bullying does not have any place in schools, or in the community.
“We want students to understand that they must be brave, and come forward and help their friends to tell the truth when something negative happens.
“I hope that the participants of the programme will share the message to their peers in their respective schools,” said Choo.
Also present were MTPN Sabah chairman cum national MTPN vice-president Kevin Lo and the council’s legal advisor Chin Tek Ming. — The Borneo Post

edd0f15b43247fe2: LUMUT: Differences of opinion over Rural and Regional Development Ministry allocations under the Finance Ministry will not affect Pakatan Harapan-Barisan Nasional political ties.
PKR Youth chief Muhammad Kamil Abdul Munim said differing approaches were normal in political cooperation and had been managed well in previous elections.

"There is no issue about it being affected. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has suggested that the issue between the ministries be coordinated harmoniously through internal discussions," he said after officiating an event at the Teluk Batik Campsite here today.
Kamil, who is political secretary to the finance minister, said Finance Ministry-level discussions will review allocation requirements and prioritise high-impact rural development projects.
The issue arose following differing statements from PH and BN leaders regarding allocations for rural development projects, raising speculation about coalition harmony ahead of the Melaka election.

It followed remarks by Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is also Rural and Regional Development Minister, concerning payment delays for contractors handling projects under his ministry.

On Wednesday (Sept 2), Treasury Secretary-General Tan Sri Johan Mahmood Merican clarified that there were no restrictions on the ministry's allocations for rural road projects, adding that constraints in contractor payments occurred because the current year's allocation had been nearly fully spent.

In a separate development, Kamil described Kepong member of parliament Lim Lip Eng's proposal for the government to consider reintroducing the Goods and Services Tax (GST) as a personal opinion based on his own analysis.
He said the government's stance remains to continue implementing the Sales and Services Tax (SST), though policies may evolve according to changing economic needs.
"For now, the government's decision is to proceed with the existing policy," he added.
5deee5d882e629f7: MELAKA: Barisan Nasional (BN) chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi has given Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh the mandate to negotiate cooperation with any party for the upcoming Melaka state election.

8a18c89e35a388c6: KOTA BHARU, Sept 6 — Six individuals — four family members and two mountain guides — who entered a forest area through Pos Dakoh, Lojing, Gua Musang on August 29 are feared missing after not leaving at Pos Kemar, Perak as scheduled on September 3.

Gua Musang district police chief Supt Sik Choon Foo said family members of the hikers lodged a police report in Selangor today after they failed to return from their hike on the set date, adding that checks with the Forestry Department showed that the last contact with the group revealed that they were in the forest area in Perak.

bc98c2aab71e8264: KYIV: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Kyiv Sunday for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after holding talks with Russia's Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on ending more than four years of war between the neighbours.
US President Donald Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner had visited Moscow several times but had not held talks in Kyiv – hit by deadly Russian strikes since 2022.
They are due to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. An AFP reporter in Kyiv saw the American envoys arrive by train.
They are hoping to revive negotiations to end Europe's worst conflict since WWII, after a summer of escalation.
Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin on Saturday to "advance President Trump's agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War," a White House official said in a statement to AFP.
"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine."
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks "extremely frank", saying the Americans "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement", but did not elaborate.
The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was "confident" it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added.
Both Russia and Ukraine have vowed not to strike each other's capitals for three days to allow for the negotiations to take place.
It was Kushner and Witkoff's eighth visit to Moscow during the war – but it is their first in the Ukrainian capital, hit by deadly Russian strikes throughout the war.
Russia's TASS news agency reported early Sunday that Witkoff and Kushner had arrived in Rzeszow in Poland on their way to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy on Sunday said Ukraine was "ready for the conversation."
"Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," the wartime leader said on social media ahead of their visit.
The country's airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war in February 2022 and visiting leaders have been arriving by train.
For many Ukrainians, hopes of a breakthrough remain slim.
"At this point it doesn't give me any hope. There have already been too many negotiations," Yaroslav, a 29-year-old Kyiv resident, told AFP.
PUTIN THANKS TRUMP
In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv – a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war.
"We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves," Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Earlier Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war despite it being "not simple."
Of the envoys' trip to Kyiv, he said: "No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial."
Trump said on Friday his envoys were bringing a "proposal" to end fighting.
"We have an idea for peace," he said, without elaborating.
US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war, and peace efforts have stalled in part because of Washington's war with Iran.
Russia occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine.
LIMITED TRUCE
Both Moscow and Kyiv committed to suspending strikes as the negotiations took place.
"The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow," Zelenskyy said.
But fighting continued elsewhere. Ukraine's air force said Russia attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it had shot down 258 drones.
On Saturday, Putin said he had "noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced" its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
However, Kyiv said that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country Saturday – including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv.

25ca2f6eb10207c7: KUALA LUMPUR: A transport policy expert has urged Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) and the Public Works Department (PWD) to diagnose the causes of congestion along Old Klang Road before deciding whether to build a proposed double-decker road or flyover.

MY Mobility Vision founder and senior adviser Wan Agyl Wan Hassan was responding to Seputeh member of parliament Teresa Kok's call for DBKL and PWD to study the need for additional road capacity along the busy Kuala Lumpur corridor.

Kok, in a Facebook post, had also urged DBKL to study worsening congestion in Bukit Jalil and Sri Petaling, particularly amid concerns over high-density development and inadequate public transport access.
Wan Agyl said Kok's call for a study was reasonable, but stressed that authorities should first identify what was causing the congestion and which solutions would remain effective in the longer term.

"Before DBKL and PWD start with the structure, they should start with the problem."What is actually causing the congestion? Which parts of the corridor are failing? And more importantly, which intervention will still work five or 10 years after it is built?" he said in a statement.
Wan Agyl said adding road capacity did not necessarily provide lasting relief, as faster journeys could attract more motorists to the route — a phenomenon known as induced demand.
However, he said a flyover could be effective if traffic modelling showed that specific junctions or conflicts between through and local traffic were causing major delays.
"Every vehicle entering an elevated road has to come down somewhere. If the next junction, merge or connecting road is already congested, we have not solved the problem. We have shifted it," he said.

He called for a comprehensive corridor mobility study covering traffic flows, major bottlenecks, local and through-traffic, public transport, parking and loading activity, as well as traffic generated by future developments.
Wan Agyl said authorities should also focus on how many people, rather than vehicles, could be moved by each intervention.
"If one project allows another 2,000 cars through a corridor, while another allows several thousand more people to travel reliably by bus, which one creates more transport capacity?" he said.

He said possible solutions should include junction improvements, traffic signal optimisation, access management, parking enforcement, improved bus services and feeder routes, with a flyover considered if supported by the evidence.
Wan Agyl also said high-density development and transport planning must be considered together, as poor public transport, walking links and feeder services could increase car dependency.
"Density itself is not the enemy. Dense development can support good public transport," he said.

He said Old Klang Road offered DBKL an opportunity to apply the principles of the Kuala Lumpur Structure Plan 2040, particularly on accessibility, efficient mobility and integrating development with public transport.

"The important thing is to diagnose first and prescribe second."If the evidence says the flyover is the best answer, build it. If the evidence points elsewhere, we should have the discipline to choose the better option," he said.
c22a34e50d42498f: SEPTEMBER 6 — The departure board says “DELAYED”. Then “CANCELLED”. Around you, children are sleeping on luggage, phones are being charged wherever a socket can be found, and somewhere beyond the airport, an Indonesian volcano is quietly changing thousands of travel plans.
If you are one of those waiting tonight, let me tell you a story.
It is a story about a very large aeroplane, a very powerful volcano and a night when nature reminded human beings that sometimes the safest journey is the one we postpone.

On June 24, 1982, British Airways Flight BA009 was flying from Kuala Lumpur towards Perth. The aircraft was a Boeing 747-200 named City of Edinburgh, cruising at around 37,000 feet above Indonesia when it entered something the crew could not see: volcanic ash from Mount Galunggung in West Java.
And here is something remarkable for Malaysian travellers sitting in an airport tonight: BA009 began its journey in Kuala Lumpur.
The passengers had expected an ordinary flight to Perth. Instead, somewhere above Indonesia, their journey became anything but ordinary.
Passengers first noticed what appeared to be smoke inside the cabin. Then came strange flashes outside the windows. The aircraft began to shake.
One engine failed.
Then another.
Then another.
Then the fourth.
All four engines were silent.

For the aviation enthusiasts among you, here is a detail worth remembering. That mighty 747 was powered by four Rolls-Royce RB211 engines — four enormous turbofans built to carry a Jumbo across oceans.
That night, all four fell silent.

Not because the aircraft was defective. Not because the pilots had made a reckless decision. A volcano had simply placed an invisible hazard directly into their flight path. Volcanic ash entered the engines, causing them to surge and eventually flame out.
For a moment, the mighty Jumbo was no longer a machine of power. It was simply a glider in the dark.

The pilots began descending. Passengers put on their oxygen masks. The cabin grew quiet. Some prayed. Some held hands. Some thought about their families. Some simply sat there, trying to understand what was happening.
And yet, remarkably, there was no mass panic.
People helped one another. Cabin crew reassured passengers. Travellers looked after children and elderly passengers. Some prayed; others simply tried to remain calm.
And the crew kept doing their job.

As the aircraft descended below the ash, the engines eventually began to come back to life. One, then another, then another. The great Rolls-Royce engines that had fallen silent began to breathe again.
The aircraft eventually landed safely in Jakarta.
Everyone survived.

Decades later, researchers interviewed some of those passengers and crew. They remembered the fear, but they also remembered kindness, responsibility, the calmness of the crew and the simple human instinct to care for one another when faced with uncertainty.
Perhaps that is the part of BA009 we should remember tonight.
If you are sitting in an Indonesian airport, waiting for a cancelled flight, you are not failing to get home.
You are waiting for the right moment to get home. There is a difference.

And if you are Malaysian, perhaps this story belongs to you a little more than you realise. Forty-four years ago, other Malaysians and travellers began their journey from Kuala Lumpur expecting to arrive in Perth. Instead, they found themselves confronting an Indonesian volcano thousands of feet above the ground.
They had a destination too.
They had somewhere they wanted to be.
And they, too, had to wait for the sky to allow them through.
So take a breath.
If your family is waiting anxiously for your message, call them. Tell them you are safe. Tell them the flight can wait. Tell them you will come home when the sky is ready.

The volcano has spoken, not with words but with ash. It has travelled through the sky and reminded us that nature does not consult our itineraries. Sometimes the departure board must surrender to something much older and more powerful than our schedules.
Tonight, perhaps, the mountain is simply asking us to wait.
Safety does not always look like movement.
Sometimes, safety looks like staying exactly where you are.

So call your mother. Call your father. Call the person waiting for you. Tell them you are all right. Hug the child beside you. Hold the hand of the person travelling with you. Share your charger with someone whose phone is dying. Let the tired child sleep.
And if you are alone, look around. You are surrounded by thousands of other people who, just like you, were supposed to be somewhere else tonight.
You are not alone in waiting.
Please remember this: a cancelled flight is an inconvenience. A flight sent into a dangerous ash cloud can become a tragedy.
The people keeping you on the ground tonight are not keeping you from your destination.
They are protecting your journey.

Forty-four years ago, a mighty Boeing 747 nearly bowed to the wrath of an Indonesian volcano. Tonight, we have something BA009's passengers did not have. We know. We can see the ash. We can track the volcano. We can close the runway.
We can wait.
And sometimes, safety is nothing more complicated than having the courage to say:
Not tonight.
So rest, traveller. Let the volcano speak. Let the ash settle. Let the engines wait.
Your destination will still be there tomorrow.
And to every Indonesian traveller waiting to continue your journey, and every Malaysian traveller longing for home:
Welcome home soon.
Not tonight, perhaps.
But soon.
And somewhere, someone who loves you is waiting to hear three simple words:
“I'm okay. I'm safe.”
Tonight, that is enough.
* Dr Marziah Zahar is a senior lecturer in Safety, Health and Environmental at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia.

559a80b44d8618ab: SEREMBAN, Sept 6 — Police confirmed a local man suspected of drug-related activities was shot dead in a residential area in Garden Homes here early this afternoon.

“Yes, I confirm the incident,” he told reporters here today.
The suspect, believed to be in his 50s, had eight previous records for drug and criminal offences. He was also wanted in connection with a case under the Kidnapping Act.

He said the neighbour reported hearing what sounded like several gunshots, though he did not hear them himself as he was indoors.

7377799318f654a2: PUTRAJAYA: A former director-general of a statutory body linked to the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda), who holds the title Datuk, is one of two people arrested by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) over alleged irregularities involving the sale of land belonging to the statutory body.
Both men, aged in their 50s and 60s, were arrested at about 4pm today after they were called to the MACC headquarters here to have their statements recorded.
They are suspected of being involved in alleged misappropriation, abuse of power and corruption in the appointment of a developer for a project in Kuala Lumpur.

He said the case was being investigated under Section 16 of the MACC Act 2009, which covers offences involving the soliciting, receiving, offering or giving of gratification as an inducement or reward in connection with a transaction or matter.

An offence under Section 16 is punishable under Section 24 of the same Act by imprisonment of up to 20 years and a fine of not less than five times the value of the gratification involved, or RM10,000, whichever is higher, upon conviction.
Earlier today, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said issues involving a Felda subsidiary would be exposed within the next few weeks.
He said the disclosure was aimed at identifying weaknesses within the institution.
Abd Halim was previously quoted as saying that he did not rule out the possibility of several individuals being detained in stages starting this week.

4c40c127c96cbeb2: GAZA CITY, Sept 6 — Palestinians held a funeral procession on Sunday for 100 people whose remains were recovered from under the rubble of destroyed homes in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood following Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave, Anadolu Ajansi (AA) reported.

Thousands of Palestinians, including relatives of the victims as well as community and political figures, attended the procession, with the remains laid out in an area near the ruins of the destroyed homes and draped in Palestinian flags.
The funeral includes memorial addresses by Gaza’s Civil Defence, whose teams carried out the recovery operations, as well as representatives of the victims’ families and community figures.
The remains are expected to be buried at Al-Ahli cemetery in the Zeitoun neighbourhood after funeral prayers.

Civil Defence teams recovered them in recent days as part of the second phase of a project launched on July 19 to retrieve the remains of Palestinians still buried beneath the rubble of buildings destroyed during the Israeli war.

The victims belonged to the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka, Qanbour and Salmi families and were killed when Israeli forces struck several residential homes around two and a half years ago, according to local authorities.

Recovery operations are being carried out with limited resources, including only a small number of excavators and deteriorating equipment, amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed to search the rubble.
Sunday’s ceremony is among the largest funerals in Palestinian history in terms of the number of bodies and remains being buried, according to an Anadolu tally.
A similar funeral was held in early August for 112 Palestinians recovered from the rubble of homes in Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood.

The second phase of the recovery project involves 800 hours of work at 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where 1,072 remains are believed to still be buried.

The first phase began in late November 2025 and involved 500 hours of work. Civil Defence teams recovered around 333 remains out of an estimated 559 missing beneath the rubble of 54 homes and buildings.

Under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, in effect since Oct 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed for recovery operations, according to Palestinian authorities in the enclave.

The ceasefire followed nearly two years of Israeli attacks on Gaza, which killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, while destroying or damaging much of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure. — Bernama-Anadolu

862b724f1305dc59: GEORGE TOWN: Gerakan Youth has urged the party not to compromise with extremism, warning that doing so could further erode support among moderate voters.

Speaking at the party's delegates' conference, Penang Gerakan Youth chief Tan Zhen Zune said Gerakan could work with any party, but must maintain its principles and draw a clear line against extremism.
He said Gerakan needed partners that were moderate, multiracial, respected the Federal Constitution and upheld the rights of all Malaysians.
"Cooperation should complement each other and seek common ground. But cooperation cannot come at the cost of losing our own principles," he said.
Tan said Gerakan also could not afford to be associated with extremist views, particularly when racial and religious issues were repeatedly raised by parties within Perikatan Nasional.

He questioned whether PN was sufficiently focused on issues affecting Malaysians' daily lives, including raising incomes, creating better jobs, assisting small and medium enterprises, retaining talent and helping young people own homes.

"If a party constantly talks about race and religion, but the people are unclear about its economic plans, surely they will ask: 'Besides race and religion, what else can PN do for our country?'" he said.

Tan said Gerakan was currently "caught in the middle", with Malay voters having larger and stronger Malay-based parties with wider grassroots networks, while non-Malay voters were increasingly finding it difficult to accept Gerakan.
He said Gerakan leaders were often left explaining or defending controversial statements made by coalition partners, while sometimes choosing to remain silent.
"The result? We have yet to truly gain Malay support, while non-Malay support is increasingly slipping away," he added.
Tan questioned Gerakan's position within PN, asking whether the party was genuinely treated as a partner or merely used to demonstrate that the coalition was multiracial.
"When it comes to policies, direction, seat allocations and major decisions, we have to honestly ask: 'To what extent is Gerakan's voice actually heard?'" he said.
He also questioned how many of Gerakan's original supporters remained with the party, how much Malay support it had actually gained, and how many moderate voters and grassroots members had been lost.
Tan said the party must also consider whether its supporters would remain loyal to Gerakan if its coalition partners no longer needed it.
"Gerakan can cooperate with anyone. But we must have principles. We must have a line," he said.
He warned that failing to address extremist statements and allowing overly conservative and extreme thinking to affect the rights of Malaysians would ultimately come at Gerakan's expense.

Tan later announced that he was stepping down as Penang Gerakan Youth chief and Gerakan Youth deputy secretary-general, saying he could no longer continue along a political path he did not believe in.
He said he had previously hoped to change the party's direction and had tried to do so, but eventually realised he was unable to bring about the change he wanted.
"I cannot continue forcing myself to accept a path that I myself do not believe in. And I cannot ask my fellow youth members to believe in something that I myself cannot convince myself of," he said.
Tan said he would submit his formal resignation letter to the Gerakan Youth secretary-general.
He apologised to delegates who might be disappointed by his decision, but said he had to remain true to his principles and take responsibility for what he believed in.
He expressed hope that Gerakan could rediscover its identity and direction before it was too late and return to being a party that genuinely represented all Malaysians.
"That is why, for me, Gerakan still needs to exist," he said.

ced28f0ed87d870e: SEPTEMBER 7 — Malaysia should not congratulate itself too quickly. But neither should it ignore something that has become increasingly apparent during the prolonged global energy crisis: the country has so far handled the fuel shock relatively well.
The contrast with parts of Asean is becoming increasingly significant.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s economic adviser, Nurhisham Hussein, said Malaysia’s fuel supply remains stable despite tightening global supplies. Petronas is confident that sufficient supplies can be secured through the end of the year.
More importantly, Malaysia has avoided the kind of severe physical shortages that an international energy crisis could easily have produced.
That is no small achievement.

But Nurhisham’s second observation deserves even greater attention. Oil prices may remain elevated for another two to three years. Countries that have drawn down their reserves are unlikely to rebuild them aggressively until prices return to something closer to US$80 a barrel.
In other words, this is no longer merely an energy-price spike.
It could become a prolonged period of expensive energy.

Malaysia enters this difficult environment with several advantages. It is a significant oil and gas producer, a net exporter of liquefied natural gas, possesses substantial domestic energy infrastructure and, above all, has Petronas.
The government has also chosen not to expose households completely to international price fluctuations.

The basic monthly eligibility for subsidised RON95 has been restored to 300 litres, with the subsidised price remaining RM1.99 per litre. Malaysia’s overall inflation, meanwhile, remains around two per cent.
This is an important economic buffer.
Petrol prices are not simply another item in the consumer price index.
Energy runs through almost everything: transportation, logistics, food distribution, manufacturing, aviation, fisheries and eventually the price of goods on supermarket shelves.
A government that prevents an international oil shock from immediately becoming a domestic cost-of-living shock therefore buys valuable economic and political breathing space.
Much of Asean is not quite so fortunate.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Motorists queue to refuel at a petrol station in Hanoi on March 10, 2026. — AFP pic
The Philippines is particularly vulnerable because of its dependence on imported energy, relatively modest buffers and rapid transmission of international energy prices into domestic costs.

Thailand is similarly exposed through its large oil and gas trade deficit. Indonesia has greater domestic energy resources but must contend with the enormous fiscal cost of shielding its population from international prices.
This is the fundamental Asean dilemma.

Governments can allow international oil prices to pass through to consumers and risk inflation, declining purchasing power and political dissatisfaction. Or they can subsidise energy heavily and transfer the shock onto government budgets.
Neither option is painless.
Indeed, fossil-fuel support across South-east Asia was estimated at US$353.1 billion in 2024 when explicit and implicit subsidies are included.
Elevated energy prices therefore represent not merely an energy-security problem but an increasingly serious fiscal challenge.
Malaysia’s relative success should consequently be understood as strategic management rather than immunity.
Kuala Lumpur still has to pay for subsidies. Businesses remain vulnerable to higher diesel, electricity, transportation and input costs.
An extended period of expensive crude could eventually work its way through supply chains regardless of government intervention.
Nor can Malaysia ignore what happens to its neighbours.

Asean is an interconnected production platform. If transportation costs rise sharply in Thailand, manufacturing costs increase in Vietnam, inflation accelerates in the Philippines or Indonesia is forced to divert billions more into energy subsidies, Malaysia will eventually feel the consequences through trade, investment and regional demand.
Energy security must therefore become an Asean issue rather than merely ten separate national problems.
The Asean Power Grid becomes even more important in this environment.
So does diversification towards renewable energy, stronger regional electricity interconnection, electric vehicles, improved public transportation and greater energy efficiency.
Interestingly, China’s rapid adoption of electric vehicles is already helping moderate global petroleum demand, according to Nurhisham.
There is a lesson here for Asean.
Energy transition should no longer be viewed exclusively through the prism of climate change. It is increasingly about strategic autonomy.

Every additional unit of electricity generated domestically from solar, hydroelectricity or other renewable sources potentially reduces exposure to distant conflicts and vulnerable maritime chokepoints.

The West Asian crisis has demonstrated brutally how geopolitical instability thousands of kilometres away can reach directly into the household budgets of South-east Asians. More than 80 per cent of the crude oil and LNG passing through the Strait of Hormuz is normally destined for Asia.
Malaysia has managed this difficult period better than might have been expected.

Stable supplies, targeted fuel support, Petronas’ international reach and relatively contained inflation have provided the country with buffers that several Asean neighbours do not possess to the same degree.
But if Nurhisham is correct that elevated oil prices could persist for another two or three years, Malaysia cannot merely congratulate itself for surviving the first stage of the crisis.
It should use the breathing space to prepare for the next one.
And Malaysia should help Asean do the same.
Energy resilience cannot stop at Malaysia’s borders. In an integrated Asean economy, Malaysia cannot remain permanently fortunate if its neighbours are increasingly unfortunate.
* Phar Kim Beng, PhD is the Professor of Asean Studies at International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS).
** This is the personal opinion of the writers or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
